what_it_does: When chip designers want to know how fast a specialized processor (like a Google TPU or AI accelerator chip) will run a given program, they currently face a frustrating tradeoff: detailed chip simulators are accurate but very slow, while fast prediction models fail badly on programs or hardware they haven't seen before. LLMulator solves this by fine-tuning a pre-trained language model (the same kind used for text generation, specifically LLaMA-3.2-1B) to predict chip performance metrics — chip area, power, and execution time — achieving 12.2% average error across diverse programs and hardware configurations, and adapting in real time to programs whose behavior changes depending on input data.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Predicting how long a program takes to run on a custom chip normally requires either running a detailed simulation (accurate but takes minutes per prediction) or training a machine-learning model on past examples (fast but fails on anything outside the training distribution). Three specific failure modes plague existing fast models: (1) programs with extreme loop sizes the model has never seen, (2) programs whose execution path changes depending on the input data (dynamic control flow), and (3) new hardware configurations not in the training set. LLMulator addresses all three.

How it works.

Part 1 — Numeric-sensitive encoding and digit-by-digit prediction. Standard language models treat a number like '1024' as a single opaque token, which breaks when a program has a loop boundary of 10,000 that the model was never trained on. LLMulator splits every number into individual digit characters before tokenizing ('1', '0', '2', '4'), so the model sees numbers the way humans do — digit by digit. Prediction is then done as a sequence of digit classifications (picking each digit 0-9) with beam search to correct errors in early digits. This lets the model extrapolate to numerical ranges well outside training data and also produces a confidence score for each prediction.

Part 2 — Online learning for input-dependent behavior. When a program's execution changes based on input (for example, a loop that runs more iterations for larger images), LLMulator runs real simulations on a handful of examples and updates the model's weights using a reinforcement-learning technique called Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Concretely: the model makes a prediction, the simulator returns the true answer, and the model is told to prefer the closer answer. A sliding window of recent examples prevents it from forgetting old knowledge. This reduces cycle-count prediction error by 41% compared to a static model.

Part 3 — Progressive training data generation. To handle new hardware configurations, the authors generate a rich training dataset automatically: first using a syntax tree tool to create basic valid programs, then mutating loops and array access patterns to look more like real accelerator code, then using another language model to diversify further. Hardware parameters (memory delays, parallelism annotations) are varied systematically. Intermediate chip design results from open-source tools (SiliconCompiler, OpenROAD) are included as 'reasoning steps' in the training examples, teaching the model to think through compilation before predicting.

The key design choice. Using digit-by-digit classification instead of a single regression output means the model is no longer forced to squeeze all possible output values through a normalization function that compresses extreme values and destroys precision at the edges.

The result. LLMulator achieves 12.2% average absolute error across 24 benchmarks, versus 28.9% for the best graph-neural-network baseline (GNNHLS) and 20.0% for the best language-model baseline (TLP).
